questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman presents with one month of worsening pedal edema. BP is 146/94, exam shows 2+ pitting edema, and urinalysis shows 4+ protein. What 24-hour urine protein threshold defines nephrotic-range proteinuria?
explanations: Incorrect. >150 mg/24 h is the upper limit of normal urine protein excretion, not the nephrotic threshold.
Incorrect. 500 mg/24 h is abnormal but well below the nephrotic threshold.
Incorrect. 1 g/24 h is abnormal proteinuria but does not meet the nephrotic definition.
Incorrect. 2 g/24 h is below the nephrotic threshold cited in the brick.
Correct. Nephrotic syndrome requires proteinuria >3.5 g/24 h (normal is <150 mg/24 h).

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with new edema is being evaluated for glomerular disease. Which tetrad of features defines full nephrotic syndrome?
explanations: Incorrect. Hematuria, HTN, and AKI describe nephritic syndrome, not nephrotic.
Correct. Nephrotic syndrome is defined by heavy proteinuria, edema, hypoalbuminemia, and hyperlipidemia.
Incorrect. RBC casts and hematuria are hallmarks of nephritic syndrome.
Incorrect. Nephrotic syndrome causes hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia, not the opposite.
Incorrect. These features describe pyelonephritis, not nephrotic syndrome.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes for 12 years presents with edema, 4+ urine protein, and a urine protein/creatinine ratio of 5. What is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in the United States?
explanations: Incorrect. Minimal change disease is the most common nephrotic disease in children, not the most common overall in the US.
Incorrect. Membranous nephropathy is a primary cause but not the most common overall.
Incorrect. Lupus nephritis is a secondary cause but not the leading cause in the US.
Correct. Diabetic kidney disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in the United States.
Incorrect. Light chain amyloidosis is an uncommon secondary cause.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with newly diagnosed nephrotic syndrome has a urinalysis with 4+ protein, no hematuria, and no RBC casts. The brick notes nephrotic syndrome is most often confused with which related glomerular syndrome characterized by hematuria?
explanations: Correct. Nephritic syndrome is the closely-named glomerular syndrome characterized by hematuria, in contrast to nephrotic syndrome's heavy proteinuria.
Incorrect. ATN is a tubular injury, not a glomerular syndrome.
Incorrect. AIN is an interstitial process, usually drug-related.
Incorrect. Pyelonephritis is an upper UTI, not a glomerular syndrome.
Incorrect. Renal artery stenosis is a vascular disease.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man undergoes renal biopsy for nephrotic syndrome. Damage at which two structures of the glomerular filtration barrier accounts for most cases of nephrotic syndrome?
choices: Tubular brush border and basement membrane
explanations: Incorrect. The mesangium and arterioles are not the principal sites of injury in nephrotic syndrome.
Incorrect. Endothelial pores allow filtration but are not the main site of injury producing nephrotic syndrome.
Correct. Most nephrotic diseases result from abnormalities of the GBM and/or the podocytes, which together form the size and negative-charge barrier.
Incorrect. The tubular brush border is not part of the glomerular filtration barrier.
Incorrect. The JGA regulates renin secretion, not filtration permeability.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with biopsy-proven nephrotic syndrome shows effaced podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy. Which property of the glomerular filter is most directly disrupted, allowing albumin to enter the urine?
explanations: Incorrect. The hydrostatic gradient is not the protein-selective barrier.
Correct. Loss of the negative charge barrier in the GBM and podocytes lets negatively charged proteins like albumin pass into the urine.
Incorrect. Tubular reabsorption is not the principal barrier preventing albumin from being filtered.
Incorrect. Mesangial contractility regulates filtration surface area, not the charge barrier.
Incorrect. The macula densa senses tubular NaCl and does not form the filtration barrier.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with nephrotic syndrome has a renal biopsy. Light microscopy is unremarkable, but electron microscopy shows diffuse podocyte foot process effacement as the only abnormality. Which diagnosis is most consistent with these findings?
explanations: Incorrect. Diabetic kidney disease shows mesangial proliferation and basement membrane thickening, not isolated effacement.
Correct. In minimal change disease, podocyte effacement is the only abnormality seen on microscopy.
Incorrect. MPGN shows GBM thickening and a tram-track appearance with immune deposits.
Incorrect. Amyloidosis shows amyloid deposits within the glomerulus, not isolated effacement.
Incorrect. FSGS shows segmental sclerosis in some glomeruli in addition to effacement.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma develops nephrotic-range proteinuria. Which mechanism best explains how myeloma causes glomerular injury?
choices: Light chain deposition in the GBM
ENaC overactivity in the collecting duct
explanations: Incorrect. Anti-PLA2 receptor antibodies are seen in membranous nephropathy, not myeloma.
Incorrect. Nonenzymatic glycation is the mechanism in diabetic kidney disease.
Correct. Neoplastic B cells secrete large amounts of light chains that filter through and damage the GBM, producing secondary nephrotic syndrome.
Incorrect. ENaC overactivity causes Liddle syndrome, not myeloma kidney disease.
Incorrect. Myeloma does not characteristically cause renal artery thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with longstanding poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has biopsy-confirmed diabetic kidney disease. Which mechanism best explains the glomerular damage?
explanations: Incorrect. Diabetic kidney disease is noninflammatory; immune complexes are not the mechanism.
Incorrect. Anti-GBM disease is a different, antibody-mediated nephritic disease.
Correct. High glucose nonenzymatic glycation of glomerular proteins plus elevated capillary hydrostatic pressure produce mesangial expansion, GBM thickening, and sclerosis.
Incorrect. Light chain deposition is the mechanism in myeloma and amyloidosis.
Incorrect. Drug toxicity is not the mechanism in diabetic kidney disease.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with biopsy-proven amyloidosis has heavy proteinuria. Which mechanism best explains her nephrotic syndrome?
choices: Amyloid light chains depositing in glomeruli
explanations: Correct. Abnormal B cells produce huge amounts of amyloid light chains that filter into and accumulate in the glomerulus, damaging the GBM.
Incorrect. Amyloidosis is a noninflammatory deposition disease, not antibody-mediated podocyte injury.
Incorrect. ENaC overexpression causes Liddle syndrome, not amyloidosis.
Incorrect. Glomerular ischemia is not the mechanism of amyloid nephropathy.
Incorrect. Tamm-Horsfall protein casts cause tubular pathology, not nephrotic-range proteinuria.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with nephrotic syndrome has serum albumin of 2.2 g/dL. Why does the liver fail to keep serum albumin normal in nephrotic syndrome?
choices: Liver synthesis is suppressed by ADH
explanations: Incorrect. ADH does not suppress hepatic albumin synthesis.
Incorrect. There is no gene silencing; the liver continues to make albumin.
Correct. Albumin lost in the urine drops the serum concentration, and the liver cannot synthesize fast enough to keep up.
Incorrect. Nephrotic syndrome is not characterized by inflammatory albumin consumption.
Incorrect. Albumin is not sequestered in the mesangium.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with nephrotic syndrome has marked lower extremity edema. Which mechanism is described in the brick as the main contributor to nephrotic edema?
explanations: Correct. The brick identifies primary renal tubular sodium retention (overfilling) as the main mechanism of nephrotic edema.
Incorrect. Increased hydrostatic pressure is not the primary mechanism in nephrotic syndrome.
Incorrect. Lymphatic obstruction causes lymphedema, not nephrotic edema.
Incorrect. Heart failure causes congestive edema by a different mechanism.
Incorrect. Hypothyroid myxedema is unrelated to nephrotic edema.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with nephrotic syndrome has hypoalbuminemia and edema. Through which secondary mechanism does hypoalbuminemia further drive sodium retention in nephrotic syndrome?
explanations: Incorrect. Hypoalbuminemia does not suppress ADH.
Incorrect. Hypoalbuminemia does not directly block ENaC.
Correct. Low oncotic pressure shifts fluid into the interstitium, lowering circulating volume and activating RAAS, which drives renal sodium reabsorption.
Incorrect. ANP would promote sodium loss, opposite of what is seen.
Incorrect. Aldosterone is stimulated, not inhibited, in this setting.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with nephrotic syndrome has total cholesterol 320 mg/dL and elevated LDL. According to the brick, which mechanism contributes to nephrotic hyperlipidemia?
explanations: Incorrect. Bile acid malabsorption is not a brick-cited mechanism.
Correct. Increased hepatic lipoprotein production, along with urinary lipoprotein loss and decreased catabolism, drives nephrotic hyperlipidemia.
Incorrect. Lipoprotein catabolism is decreased, not increased.
Incorrect. Diet is not the mechanism cited in the brick.
Incorrect. Pancreatic insufficiency is unrelated to nephrotic hyperlipidemia.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with newly diagnosed nephrotic syndrome develops a left lower extremity DVT. Loss of which class of urinary proteins best explains her thrombotic risk?
explanations: Incorrect. Loss of IgG predisposes to infection, not thrombosis.
Correct. Loss of anticoagulant proteins (e.g., antithrombin) in the urine increases the risk of DVT, renal vein thrombosis, and PE.
Incorrect. Acute phase reactants are not the relevant lost protein.
Incorrect. Albumin loss causes hypoalbuminemia and edema, not thrombosis directly.
Incorrect. Apolipoprotein loss contributes to dyslipidemia, not thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with nephrotic syndrome develops Streptococcus pneumoniae peritonitis. Loss of which urinary protein best explains his susceptibility to infection?
explanations: Incorrect. Antithrombin loss predisposes to thrombosis, not infection.
Incorrect. Albumin loss leads to edema, not increased infection risk.
Correct. Loss of IgG in the urine renders nephrotic patients more susceptible to infection.
Incorrect. Transferrin loss can contribute to anemia but is not the brick's stated reason for infection risk.
Incorrect. Ceruloplasmin loss is not cited as a cause of infection susceptibility.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with new lower extremity edema has 4+ proteinuria on dipstick. The dipstick test detects which urinary protein?
explanations: Incorrect. The dipstick does not detect positively charged proteins like immunoglobulin light chains.
Correct. The urine dipstick detects only urinary albumin; nephrotic syndrome typically shows 4+.
Incorrect. Tamm-Horsfall protein is not detected by the dipstick.
Incorrect. Hemoglobin reacts with the blood pad, not the protein pad.
Incorrect. Myoglobin is detected on the blood pad, not the protein pad.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with multiple myeloma has bony pain and fatigue. His urine dipstick is negative for protein, yet a 24-hour collection reveals 5 g of protein. Why might the dipstick miss his urinary protein?
explanations: Correct. The urine dipstick detects only albumin and misses positively charged urinary proteins like immunoglobulin light chains seen in myeloma.
Incorrect. The dipstick is the standard test for albumin.
Incorrect. The issue is selectivity, not sensitivity.
Incorrect. Light chains are not completely reabsorbed in myeloma.
Incorrect. The dipstick does not require alkaline urine to detect protein.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman has 4+ urine protein on dipstick. According to the brick, which spot urine protein/creatinine ratio is consistent with nephrotic-range proteinuria?
explanations: Incorrect. 0.15 is the upper limit of normal.
Incorrect. Above the normal range but below the nephrotic cutoff.
Incorrect. 1.0 indicates significant proteinuria but is below the nephrotic range.
Incorrect. 2.0 is heavy proteinuria but still below the nephrotic threshold.
Correct. A spot urine protein/creatinine ratio >3.5 (or >3.5 g on a 24-hour collection) indicates nephrotic-range proteinuria.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with nephrotic-range proteinuria has a urinalysis that also shows dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts. What does this combination of findings suggest?
explanations: Incorrect. Dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts are not features of pure nephrotic syndrome.
Correct. Hematuria, dysmorphic RBCs, and RBC casts indicate an overlapping nephritic component (e.g., lupus nephritis, MPGN).
Incorrect. UTI typically has pyuria and bacteriuria, not RBC casts.
Incorrect. Renal calculi cause hematuria but not RBC casts or nephrotic-range proteinuria.
Incorrect. Bladder cancer causes painless hematuria but not the RBC casts or proteinuria pattern described.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with biopsy-proven membranous nephropathy is undergoing serologic workup. Which antibody is most strongly associated with primary membranous nephropathy?
explanations: Incorrect. Anti-GBM is associated with Goodpasture syndrome.
Incorrect. ANCA is associated with vasculitides such as GPA.
Correct. Anti-PLA2 receptor antibodies are positive in primary membranous nephropathy.
Incorrect. Anti-dsDNA is associated with lupus nephritis.
Incorrect. ASO titers are associated with post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old previously healthy boy presents with sudden-onset facial and lower extremity edema, 4+ urine protein, and serum albumin 1.8 g/dL. Per the brick, what is the next step?
explanations: Correct. In young children, minimal change disease is the most likely cause, and empiric prednisone is given without biopsy; treatment response confirms the diagnosis.
Incorrect. Biopsy is generally not done in children with new nephrotic syndrome because of the high pre-test probability of minimal change disease.
Incorrect. Cyclophosphamide is not first-line in pediatric nephrotic syndrome.
Incorrect. Plasmapheresis is not the standard initial therapy in this setting.
Incorrect. Observation alone is not appropriate for a child with overt nephrotic syndrome.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman with 12 years of poorly controlled diabetes, retinopathy, and proteinuria of 6 g/24 h is being managed for presumed diabetic nephropathy. Per the brick, when is renal biopsy generally NOT required?
explanations: Incorrect. Lupus nephritis usually requires biopsy to define class.
Incorrect. Membranous nephropathy is typically diagnosed by biopsy.
Correct. Diabetic kidney disease has a predictable pattern and clear underlying cause, and biopsy is usually unnecessary.
Incorrect. FSGS requires biopsy for diagnosis.
Incorrect. MPGN requires biopsy to confirm.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with newly diagnosed nephrotic syndrome has BP 138/86. Which medication class should all adult patients with nephrotic syndrome receive, regardless of blood pressure?
explanations: Incorrect. Beta-blockers are not recommended for all nephrotic patients.
Incorrect. CCBs lower blood pressure but do not provide the antiproteinuric and renoprotective effects.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics treat edema but are not given to all nephrotic patients regardless of BP.
Correct. All adults with nephrotic syndrome (or any abnormal proteinuria) should receive an ACE inhibitor or ARB to lower BP, lower proteinuria, and slow progression, regardless of starting BP.
Incorrect. Thiazides are used for hypertension and edema but are not the universally recommended renoprotective class.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with chronic nephrotic syndrome has LDL of 180 mg/dL and total cholesterol of 290 mg/dL. Per the brick, which medication is recommended to reduce his cardiovascular risk?
explanations: Incorrect. Niacin is not the brick's recommended therapy for nephrotic hyperlipidemia.
Incorrect. Fibrates target triglycerides and are not the brick's recommendation.
Correct. Statins should be used to control hyperlipidemia in chronic nephrotic syndrome because of the increased risk of atherosclerotic disease and cardiovascular mortality.
Incorrect. Bile acid sequestrants are not the recommended therapy in this setting.
Incorrect. Omega-3 fatty acids are not the brick's recommendation.
